title: Witr in many ways
hook: one, three, or more units, prayed in different ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, the moon, and your line: which moon? Did you find out how your local calendar decides when a month begins? Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

It's late. The house is dark except for one lamp. Someone who has already prayed the night prayer stands up once more before bed, for one last short prayer. In one home that last prayer is three units, with a quiet supplication tucked inside the third. In another it's a single unit, standing alone. In a third, two units, a pause and a greeting of peace, and then one more. All three people would tell you the same thing: they're closing the night with an odd number. Today, witr, the odd prayer, and the many ways to pray it.
screen: `ONE LAMP, ONE LAST PRAYER.` → `THREE, OR ONE, OR TWO THEN ONE.` → `ALWAYS AN ODD NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Witr means odd, the opposite of even. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that Allah is witr, one, and loves what is odd. The prayer carries the same word. Next, the instruction. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar reports the Prophet's answer: the night prayer is prayed two units by two, and when someone fears the dawn is near, they pray one unit to make the whole odd. And in Sunan Abi Dawud, a report gives the choice outright: whoever wishes may pray witr with five, or with three, or with one. The odd number is fixed. The shape is open. Then, the schools. Hanafi scholars teach that witr is wajib, a duty just below the obligatory prayers, prayed as three units joined together with one closing greeting, and a supplication, the qunut, before bowing in the third. Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars count it as a strongly encouraged sunna; its smallest form is a single unit, and three may be prayed as two, a greeting, then one. Maliki teaching has a single unit of witr, following a pair of units prayed first. In the Ja'fari school, witr is a single unit that closes the night prayer, with a qunut of its own. Last, the thread. Each of these is odd. Each closes the night. The people in those three homes are standing at different angles to the same instruction, and each can show you the report they're standing on. Odd, in any way.
screen: `WITR: ODD, NOT EVEN.` · `TWO BY TWO, THEN ONE.` · `FIVE, THREE, OR ONE.` · `EACH SCHOOL'S SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray your witr, or close your day with something odd. If you pray, tonight before sleep, pray witr in the way your school teaches, and notice how it closes the night. If you don't, try this now: count three slow breaths, and let the third be the longest, the one that closes the set. Then rest. Later, before bed, do it again, three breaths, the last one longest, a small odd number at the end of the day. The bell holds the time.
Witr in many ways. The odd prayer that closes the night: one, three or more units, prayed in each school's own shape. Today's word.

Your line: odd, in any way. This week: the plain sense, the Amman Message, hands, amin, touch, the moon, and witr. Tonight, close the day with something small and odd. Tomorrow, the doors between the schools. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Witr is prayed after the night prayer and before dawn: Hanafis as three joined units with qunut, treating it as wajib; Shafi'is and Hanbalis as one or more odd units, often two and then one; Malikis as one unit after a pair; Ja'fari Shia as a single unit with qunut closing the night prayer.

original.note: Arabic: odd, single; the name of the odd-numbered prayer that closes the night.

trapdoor: what you thought: witr is one fixed prayer prayed the same way by everyone.
what it means: witr is any odd closing to the night prayer, and each school has its own shape for it.
what a scholar hears: wajib against sunna mu'akkada, qunut before or after bowing, joined three against two and one, and Ibn Umar's two by two.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2677 (Allah is witr and loves witr)
Sahih al-Bukhari 990 (Ibn Umar: the night prayer two by two; one to make it odd)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1422 (witr with five, three or one)

notes: Editor: Ibn Umar's report now attributed as the Prophet's answer; 'the prayer takes its name from that' (the hadith) changed to 'carries the same word'; 'often prayed' softened; duplicate week look-back cut from the teach (kept in the carry).
Muslim 2677, Bukhari 990, Abu Dawud 1422: confirm numbers and paraphrases. Abu Dawud 1422 opens by calling witr a duty (haqq) on every Muslim; the script gives only the choice of five, three or one.

School positions: Hanafi wajib, three joined units with one taslim, qunut before ruku' in the third; Shafi'i/Hanbali sunna mu'akkada, minimum one, three often prayed 2+1; Maliki one unit after shaf'; Ja'fari a single unit concluding salat al-layl, with qunut. Confirm each.
Trapdoor floor 3 mentions qunut before or after bowing: Hanafi before ruku'; Shafi'i/Hanbali after; confirm.
